newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Steel workers attack bank on Thyssen/Krupp.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Steel workers attack bank on Thyssen/Krupp.

text.p: Steel workers fearing for their jobs turned their ire on Germany's powerful banks on Monday for their role in backing a takeover bid by Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp for Thyssen AG.
Waving banners reading "Banks: Hands off Thyssen" and "Tell the bankers to shut up," several hundred Thyssen workers demonstrated at a Deutsche Bank AG branch in Duesseldorf.
Deutsche Bank, Dresdner Bank AG and U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs have backed Krupp's bid for rival Thyssen. With other banks, it will provide funding if the deal goes through.
Engineering union IG Metall vowed that 30,000 protesters would march on Germany's financial capital, Frankfurt, on Tuesday to protest against any deal involving major job losses.

Krupp has agreed to suspend the hostile bid pending talks with Thyssen on a possible merger of their steel operations. But it has said it will revive the bid if the talks do not yield fruit by a Thursday deadline.
The Duesseldorf protesters blamed the banks for fostering a deal expected to eliminate at least 7,000 jobs at Germany's two largest steel makers.
"If the banks use such brutal practices, you have to take to the streets," Jens Peter Schmidt, who works at Thyssen's Rheinstahltechnik unit, told Reuters Television.

They have been accused by politicians and union leaders of joining a corporate raid that goes against the grain of Germany's consensus culture and which could cause heavy job losses at a time of record postwar unemployment.
IG Metall demanded that Krupp and Thyssen rule out large-scale job losses as part of any deal, including 2,200 job cuts Krupp has announced under a restructuring of its steel unit.
"An indispensable precondition of an acceptable solution is the ruling out of mass layoffs," the union said in a statement.
Deutsche Bank has borne the brunt of criticism because its management board member Ulrich Cartellieri is represented on Thyssen's supervisory board. He did not inform it of Krupp's impending bid.
"It would be good for the German economy if a world-class industrial concern emerged" from a merger, he said in a statement as top executives continued negotiations.
"Only then can the incessant job reductions in both firms come to end."
Cartellieri rejected criticism from workers and politicians that he did not inform Thyssen of Krupp's bid.
Tipping off Thyssen would have been "an inadmissible use of business information of third parties", he said.

Cartellieri's favourable view of a merger followed other positive comments at the weekend. Thyssen chief Dieter Vogel, who originally condemned the "Wild West" tactics behind Krupp's hostile bid, told workers the talks were going well.

Wolfgang Clement, economics minister of the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, also said on Sunday he expected the firms to reach a cooperative agreement. Germany's steel industry is based in the state.
Thyssen agreed to a week of negotiations on a joint steel company after Krupp's surprise bid of 435 marks ($257) per Thyssen share, 25 percent more than the price at the time.

Thyssen shares rose 26.50 marks to 417 marks on Monday after reports said Thyssen planned to ward off any renewed Krupp bid by telling shareholders the stock had the potential to rise to at least 550 marks.
Thyssen's supervisory board has already called a meeting for Thursday, possibly in expectation of an agreed deal emerging by the time the deadline expires, workers said.

Thyssen management on Monday distanced itself from the union demonstrations, saying it was not participating in or financing Tuesday's protest in Frankfurt. "It is a union event," the company said in a statement.
The union planned to march through Frankfurt and gather in front of Deutsche Bank's headquarters at midday (1100 GMT).
($ = 1.691 German Marks)
